title: Spanish Grand Prix briefing: Antonelli wins, Norris’ pitstop woes, Hamilton’s DNF
content:
MADRID, Spain — Kimi Antonelli won the first Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring ahead of Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, after a brief virtual safety car period split the field onto opposing strategies and undid a race Norris had been controlling from pole position.

The win stretches Antonelli’s world championship points lead over his Mercedes teammate George Russell from 66 points to 81, while Mercedes leads the constructors’ standings on 503 points, 145 clear of Ferrari, with nine rounds remaining in the 2026 season.

“Let’s keep pushing,” Antonelli said over his team radio after the win.

At the start, Norris converted his pole into the lead and led by 6.2 seconds on Lap 14 of 57. But when Lance Stroll stopped at Turn 20, the VSC was activated to slow the field, and Norris was too far around the circuit to reach the pit lane in time. Most of those behind immediately — Antonelli, Verstappen and Russell — took cheap pit stops under the reduced speeds.

Norris did come in a lap later, just after the race had gone green again, and he then lost more time to a slow pit stop, emerging in fifth place. The sequence cost him a race he had firmly in hand.

Charles Leclerc, who had started on hard tires, stayed out, inheriting the lead and then holding it for more than 30 laps as the compound proved far more durable than forecast in 52-degree Celsius track temperatures. Ferrari gambled on holding track position and waiting for a late safety car period that never came; the race ran green from Lap 15 to the finish. Leclerc pitted on Lap 49 for fresh soft tires and rejoined in fourth place.

Mercedes went the other way with Russell, pitting him a second time on Lap 29 despite his arguments for a single stop. “Why did we pit? I could have held Norris off,” he asked over the radio, by then 30 seconds adrift of the podium fight. He took the fastest lap as consolation.

Norris recovered to hound Verstappen through the closing stages, twice getting within a second of the Red Bull before locking his brakes on Lap 55 dropped him out of range.

Lewis Hamilton played no part. He reported he had no brakes and could not accelerate for fear of being unable to stop, so he fell from fourth to last inside six laps before retiring on Lap 9.

The Athletic’s Madeline Coleman and Luke Smith analyze the key talking points.

Not all races can be won with a charge from 19th on the grid to a sensational and emotional home victory, as Antonelli did last Sunday at Monza. Sometimes, it’s about being in the right place to grab the opportunity when your rivals stumble.

Without the timing of the VSC for Stroll’s stricken Aston Martin, Antonelli may not have won in Madrid. Norris had pulled out a six-second buffer at the front that was growing in the early stages, giving him control of the race at the front before the unfortunate timing of the VSC and a slow stop dropped him out of the fight.

It handed Antonelli the net lead, one he partly gained thanks to Red Bull’s instruction that Verstappen give Hamilton a position back for an off-track move at Turn 1, which also meant to had to allow the Mercedes through.

Antonelli had to keep an eye on not overheating his brakes by getting too close to Leclerc prior to the Ferrari pitting, as well as flirting with track limits breaches (his only real weakness this year.) But he otherwise drove a very mature and straightforward race, enough to capture yet another win after moving back to the front once Leclerc finally pitted. Verstappen had closed to sit just a second behind, but was never close enough to seriously go for a move to win.

With Hamilton retiring early and Russell only fifth, the win has given Antonelli another big boost to his already-healthy points lead.

It’s these kind of races upon which a championship is built at this point of the run-in.

Another race, another win, and another step on the road to crowning F1’s youngest world champion. Antonelli can’t go far wrong right now. — Luke Smith

Norris’ weekend hasn’t exactly been clean. The Briton missed FP2 due to a gearbox issue, costing him critical track time at this new circuit. Yet, he managed to put together a magical lap in qualifying that put him on pole position for Sunday’s race — despite nearly hitting the barriers at the last corner.

He went as far as calling it the “perfect lap” up until that corner and it set Norris up well for Sunday’s race.

An interesting trend emerged during the Formula Two and Formula Three races Saturday, where the person in second took the lead. But that wasn’t the case in F1. Norris retained the lead and held onto it until the first round of pit stops.

The VSC period led to numerous drivers taking a cheaper pit stop. The speed limit around a track is lower during these periods, which means taking a pit stop (especially in a pit lane this long) isn’t as costly. Norris stayed out the first time around, as he was past the pit entry, but McLaren called him in for the next lap — only the VSC ended as the Briton headed into the pits.

Norris endured a slower than usual pit stop and subsequently fell down the order to fifth when he rejoined the pack. He moved up the sequence as Russell pitted, the Mercedes driver swapping out his medium tires for a set of hards.

By Lap 42, Norris had caught up to Verstappen, who was running third, and less than a second separated them as the McLaren driver pushed. He moved up the order to a podium finish, third-place, with Leclerc pitting on Lap 49. — Madeline Coleman

The slow fade of Hamilton’s bid for an eighth world championship — one that admittedly always seemed a bit of a long shot, given Antonelli and Mercedes’ advantage — took its biggest hit of the season.

One week on from the close moment with Leclerc at Monza that flared tensions and led to internal talks, Hamilton suffered his first retirement of the season to compound a disappointing weekend for Ferrari.

Although he’d made a good getaway from the line and been dicing with Verstappen on the opening lap, Hamilton quickly reported that he was struggling with a possible brake failure, eventually proven as he went off the track and into one of the run-off areas. Clearly his race was run, resigning him to his first zero-points half of the season.

Speaking to Sky Sports in the media pen after the race, Hamilton admitted there was “no stopping” Antonelli and Mercedes this year, praising their form.

The VSC did at least give Ferrari a chance to roll the dice on Leclerc’s strategy, keeping him out on a set of hard tires to move into the lead. He ran 48 laps on that set of tires, leading more of the race than any other driver, the hope being that a safety car period or red flag could play into their hands. Ferrari ultimately pitted Leclerc with 10 laps to go, giving him fourth.

While Ferrari never looked like it had the outright fastest car in Madrid, to leave without a podium finish caps off a disappointing double-header for the Italian team. — Luke Smith

If you listened to the drivers’ comments during media day on Thursday, you would’ve expected chaos to have unfolded from the get-go. And it seemed like a safe bet at the time, given the nature of the circuit and how the junior categories fared.

Take F3’s test, where there were double-digit red flags across the multi-day testing. Even as F3 and F2’s sessions unfolded in Madrid this weekend, it wasn’t clean, and neither were F1’s. Hamilton, Arvid Lindblad and Ollie Bearman all had incidents throughout practice, and Bearman’s was so severe that he couldn’t participate in qualifying due to the damage his car suffered.

But come Sunday, F1’s first grand prix at Madring turned into a procession, with no raging chaos that upended the grid unless you count a few car-related retirements or a few close racing moments at the start.

It ended up being like the 2016 Azerbaijan GP, the first race at Baku. Many expected chaos because of how the F2 race went, but the race that year was calm.

The main ‘edge-of-your-seat’ moment came in the final eight laps or so, after Leclerc pitted. The top three drivers were covered by over two seconds, but Antonelli began pulling away from Verstappen and Norris.

One of the big drawbacks of the track are the limited overtaking opportunities, something several drivers pointed out during post-qualifying media sessions, and the pit lane is quite long, which means teams possibly were less inclined to spice up their strategies so they wouldn’t lose too much time.

This is just year one at Madring. Time will tell if they listen to the feedback from fans, drivers and teams and make adjustments. — Madeline Coleman
